content:
A comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) is a detailed, joined-up check of an older person's health and daily life. It looks at physical health, mobility, medicines, memory, mood and the support you have at home, and leads to a care plan agreed with you. If you live with arthritis and frailty, a CGA can bring together all your conditions and medicines, rather than treating each one separately.

This guide explains what a CGA covers, who carries it out, and how to prepare. It is educational information, not a diagnosis.

What a CGA is

The British Geriatrics Society describes CGA as a process that assesses an older person's medical, functional, psychological and social needs, and then plans and follows up care. It is often led by a geriatrician (a doctor who specialises in older people's health), but GPs, nurses, therapists and pharmacists may all be involved. It can happen in hospital, in a clinic, at your GP surgery or at home.

What it usually covers

  • Physical health: your conditions, including arthritis, heart and lung problems, and continence.
  • Medicines: a review of everything you take, looking for side effects, interactions and medicines that may no longer be needed.
  • Mobility and falls: walking, balance, transfers and any falls.
  • Memory and mood: checks for memory problems, low mood or anxiety.
  • Nutrition: weight, appetite and eating.
  • Daily living and home: washing, dressing, cooking, and whether your home suits you.
  • Support and wishes: family and carers, and what matters most to you.

Why it matters if you have arthritis

Arthritis pain can look like frailty, and frailty can make arthritis harder to manage. A CGA helps separate the two and spot treatable problems, such as a medicine causing dizziness, poorly controlled pain, low vitamin D or an untreated infection. It can also link you to physiotherapy, occupational therapy and equipment.

How to get a CGA

Ask your GP whether a CGA or referral to an older people's or frailty service would help, especially if you have several conditions, take lots of medicines, have had falls, or notice changes in memory or continence. In hospital, the ward team may arrange one. Services vary by area.

How to prepare

  • Bring all your medicines, including creams, inhalers and anything bought over the counter.
  • Write down your main concerns and what has changed recently.
  • Note any falls, near misses or changes in weight.
  • Bring someone who knows you well, if you can.
  • Think about what matters most to you, such as staying at home or getting out to see friends.

After the assessment

You should agree a care plan, with clear actions and who is responsible for each. Ask for a copy, and ask who to contact if things change. Follow-up is an important part of CGA.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day for sudden confusion or a sudden drop in mobility over hours or days.
  • See your GP for unplanned weight loss, repeated falls or a steady decline over weeks.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Do I need a geriatrician as well as a rheumatologist?

Not always. Many people are supported by their GP and community teams. A CGA may help if medicines are stacking up, falls are repeating or memory is changing.

Is a CGA a test I can fail?

No. It is a way of understanding your needs and planning care with you.

Will it change my arthritis treatment?

It might, for example by adjusting painkillers or adding physiotherapy. Any changes should be discussed with you and your arthritis team.
